ai.definition: Consciousness Uploads involve the precise mapping of an individual's brain activity and neural patterns, followed by their replication in a virtual or digital environment. This process aims to preserve or transfer conscious experiences from a biological mind to a non-biological substrate.
ai.howItWorks: The technology employs advanced neuroimaging techniques to capture the intricate details of brain functions at a cellular level. These data are then used to create highly detailed neural models, which serve as the basis for simulating and replicating conscious experiences using sophisticated AI algorithms. The goal is to accurately represent not just cognitive processes but also subjective experiences such as emotions and perceptions.
ai.problemSolved: Consciousness Uploads address the challenge of long-term human existence by providing a means to preserve or transfer consciousness beyond the confines of physical bodies, potentially overcoming limitations imposed by aging and mortality.
ai.manufacturing: Currently in the conceptual phase, no large-scale manufacturing processes exist. The technology requires highly specialized equipment for neuroimaging and advanced AI systems for data analysis and simulation.
ai.buildProcess: The build process involves multiple stages: initial brain scanning to gather neural data, model creation using computational tools, and validation through iterative testing of simulated experiences against real-world inputs and outputs.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the high cost of neuroimaging equipment, the complexity of AI algorithms needed for accurate simulation, and the need for extensive computational resources. Additionally, ethical considerations and regulatory compliance add significant overhead.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is highly speculative given current technological limitations and ethical concerns. However, if breakthroughs occur in neuroimaging resolution and AI capabilities, this technology could transition into early commercial stages within the next few decades.
ai.regulation: Current regulatory frameworks do not address consciousness uploads comprehensively. The development of such technologies would likely necessitate new legislation to govern issues related to privacy, consent, and ethical use.
ai.risks: Risks include potential inaccuracies in neural data interpretation, security vulnerabilities in digital storage of consciousness, and the possibility of unintended consequences from altering or replicating human experiences.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to the speculative nature of the technology. If successful, it could open up new markets for healthcare, entertainment, and education but would require significant investment in both research and infrastructure development.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may involve advancements in neurotechnology, AI, and data processing capabilities that could make consciousness uploads more feasible. Ethical frameworks and regulatory policies will also play crucial roles in shaping the future of this technology.

glossary.def: The process of transferring an individual's consciousness or mind into a digital or virtual environment.
Detailed representations of brain structures and functions used to simulate conscious experiences in computational environments.
Computer programs designed to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as pattern recognition and decision-making.

subsystems.name: Connectome mapping
subsystems.role: obtain a complete wiring diagram of every neuron and synapse in a brain.

subsystems.name: Functional state capture
subsystems.role: record the dynamic activity and molecular environment of all neurons at a moment in time.

subsystems.name: Computational model
subsystems.role: translate the wiring diagram and activity into a mathematical simulation of neural dynamics.

subsystems.name: Simulation hardware
subsystems.role: run the whole-brain model fast enough to behave in real time.

subsystems.name: Consciousness theory and validation
subsystems.role: determine which features of the simulation are necessary for subjective experience.
parts: theories of consciousness (e.g. integrated information, global workspace)

subsystems.name: Interface and embodiment
subsystems.role: provide sensory input and motor output so the uploaded mind can interact with a world.

buildSteps.title: Map the connectome
buildSteps.detail: A brain is fixed, sliced into nanometre-thin sections, imaged by electron microscopy, and reconstructed by software into a complete map of neurons and synapses. This has been done for the 302-neuron worm C. elegans and parts of larger brains, but never for a mammal at full scale.

buildSteps.title: Capture the functional state
buildSteps.detail: At the moment of scanning, the activity level, receptor states and molecular concentrations of every neuron must be recorded. Current techniques sample only tiny fractions of a brain, so this step would need entirely new non-destructive, whole-brain recording methods.

buildSteps.title: Build a computational model
buildSteps.detail: The connectome and state are converted into a simulation where each neuron and synapse is represented by equations. The model must reproduce the brain's electrical and chemical behaviour, not just its wiring.

buildSteps.title: Run the simulation
buildSteps.detail: A supercomputer or dedicated neuromorphic hardware executes the model. Simulating a human brain in real time is estimated to require far more computing power than any machine today, though the exact requirement is unknown.

buildSteps.title: Validate for consciousness
buildSteps.detail: Researchers would test whether the simulation reports subjective experiences, learns, and behaves like the original person. Because no scientific test for consciousness exists, this step is currently unverifiable.

buildSteps.title: Connect senses and actions
buildSteps.detail: The simulated mind is linked to a virtual world or robotic body through brain–computer interfaces, so it can see, hear, speak and move. Today's interfaces handle only simple signals, not full sensory-motor immersion.

buildSteps.title: Stabilise and maintain
buildSteps.detail: The uploaded mind must remain coherent over years, able to learn and adapt without drifting into malfunction. No one knows whether a digital copy would stay stable or degrade.

prerequisites.tech: Whole-brain connectome mapping at synaptic resolution
prerequisites.why: only small organisms like C. elegans have been fully mapped; a human brain has about 86 billion neurons and trillions of synapses.

prerequisites.tech: Non-destructive functional recording of every neuron
prerequisites.why: existing tools record from thousands of neurons at best, not the entire brain simultaneously.
without knowing what physical processes produce subjective experience, we cannot know if a simulation is conscious.
the fastest supercomputers now reach exascale, but real-time whole-brain simulation is thought to need orders of magnitude more.
current implants restore limited movement or communication, not full sensory and motor embodiment.

pathway.milestone: complete connectomes of small organisms and partial maps of mammalian brains
pathway.unlocks: basic understanding of how neural wiring relates to behaviour.

pathway.milestone: full connectome and functional recording of a mouse brain
pathway.unlocks: the first realistic whole-brain simulations of a mammal.

pathway.milestone: simulation of a mouse brain that reproduces learned behaviours
pathway.unlocks: confidence that digital models can capture complex brain function.

pathway.milestone: human brain mapping and simulation, if ethical and technical barriers are overcome
pathway.unlocks: a testbed for consciousness theories and, speculatively, a route to mind uploading.

pathway.milestone: validated consciousness transfer and long-term stability
pathway.unlocks: digital minds that could be stored, copied or embodied — a profound ethical and philosophical shift.
